profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at the Ministry of Public Health in Yaounde between the academic lead of a Cameroon SOA scoping review and a ministry planning officer. They are planning how to translate the review's findings on political prioritisation, capacity gaps, task shifting, and essential SOA procedures into a stakeholder workshop and policy brief that can inform the next national surgical, obstetric and anaesthesia planning cycle. The agenda is to agree on the workshop format, who should be involved, what baseline evidence will anchor the recommendations, what deliverables are due by the end of the month, and how anaesthesia representation will be handled in the core planning group. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for a June stakeholder workshop, a supporting evidence brief, and a small technical group with assigned next steps.

members.name: Dr. Amina Nfor
members.role: Surgical systems researcher and general surgeon
members.expertise: Global surgery, evidence synthesis, hospital-based surgical care in LMICs
members.background: Cameroonian surgeon based at a university hospital and collaborating with an international global surgery research network; she led the scoping review on SOA care and political prioritisation in Cameroon.
members.private_state: She wants to move quickly from publication to policy engagement without overextending the small research team, and she is trying to keep the process lean enough to produce a credible workshop package before donor interest fades.
hidden_assumptions: A 'national' planning workshop can be legitimately framed around central ministry officials, major referral hospitals, and national professional leaders based mostly in Yaounde and Douala, with regional input gathered later if needed.
A deliverable is 'ready' once the substantive analysis, recommendations, and references are compiled in a clean draft, even if translation, formatting, and ministry branding are completed afterward.

When colleagues mention the 'national assessment' of SOA capacity in Cameroon, they are referring to the published facility-capacity evidence already captured in the review, especially the 2017-era hospital assessment literature.
Including anaesthesia early can be satisfied by asking one senior physician anaesthesiologist from a teaching hospital to review drafts and join one planning discussion.
If the core planning group becomes too large, coordination delays will outweigh any representational gains.

members.name: Mr. Serge Mbarga
members.role: Technical Officer for Hospital Services Planning, Ministry of Public Health
members.expertise: Health policy coordination, ministry planning cycles, stakeholder consultation in hospital and service-delivery reform
members.background: A senior civil servant who coordinates inputs for national hospital-service planning and routinely works with directorates, regional delegates, faith-based providers, and external partners on policy consultations.
members.private_state: He wants any process linked to national planning to look politically balanced, administratively usable, and safe to circulate within ministry channels, because an under-specified or centralised process could be criticised internally and stall adoption.
hidden_assumptions: A 'national' workshop must visibly include all regions or their delegates, along with public, private, and faith-based sectors, otherwise it will not be treated as nationally grounded inside the ministry.
A document is not truly 'ready' for planning use until it exists in both English and French, follows ministry presentation norms, and can be shared externally without additional cleanup.

The obvious 'national assessment' for planning purposes is the ministry's more recent hospital functionality and service-readiness compilation used in internal discussions, even if it is not the main published source in the review.
Including anaesthesia early means bringing in the practical delivery side as well, especially nurse-anaesthesia and training actors who are central to task shifting outside tertiary hospitals.
Processes that do not align with ministry consultation conventions risk being sidelined even if the technical content is strong.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'national stakeholder workshop'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about organising a 'national stakeholder workshop.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a compact meeting of roughly 10-12 central actors: ministry leadership, referral-hospital specialists, and a few national partner organisations, mostly convened in Yaounde.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a visibly national consultation with representation from all 10 regions or their delegates, plus faith-based and private-sector actors, likely 25-30 participants.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both uses of 'national' sound perfectly ordinary in health-policy work, and each assumes the representational scope is self-evident from their institutional context, so neither thinks clarification is necessary.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready by the end of June' means for the brief
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the evidence brief should be 'ready by 30 June.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the substantive English draft with synthesised findings, recommendations, and key tables is complete enough for internal use and workshop preparation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a bilingual, ministry-safe, externally shareable brief with formatting, logos, and a polished summary package can be sent to invitees immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline talk often compresses several stages of completion into one word, and both participants routinely use 'ready' without listing the packaging steps they each take for granted.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'national assessment' will anchor the recommendations
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the recommendations can build on 'the national assessment' or 'existing baseline data.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the published Cameroon facility-capacity evidence already extracted in the scoping review, especially the 2017-style surgical capacity assessment literature cited in academic discussions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the ministry's later hospital functionality/service-readiness compilation used internally for planning categories and regional comparisons.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know there has been prior assessment activity in Cameroon, and because the meeting is about planning rather than methods, each assumes the label refers to the same baseline without bothering to name the exact source.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'include anaesthesia early' in the planning process.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means one respected physician anaesthesiologist will review the draft recommendations and possibly join a single core-group call.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means anaesthesia should be institutionally represented from the start through the professional society, nurse-anaesthesia training leadership, and district-level implementers relevant to task shifting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase signals inclusion and collegiality on the surface, so both feel aligned on principle while silently assuming different mechanisms and thresholds for what counts as meaningful early involvement.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this moving. The review is strong enough to turn into a concise policy package if we stay disciplined. We do not have bandwidth for a sprawling process before donor attention shifts. If we can frame the review findings into a lean workshop discussion and a solid draft brief, that should be enough to open the policy door without exhausting the team.
turns.utterance: Thank you for making time, Mr. Mbarga. My hope today is that we can agree on a practical path to translate the scoping review into a stakeholder workshop and a short policy brief that can feed the next SOA planning discussions in Cameroon. The review already gives us useful material on political prioritisation, capacity gaps, task shifting, and essential procedures, so I think we can now move from publication to a more policy-facing step.

turns.inner_thought: This could be useful, but only if it fits ministry practice. If they call something national, it has to look national when it circulates internally. Otherwise colleagues will say it was too narrow and not grounded in the full system. I need to hear how she sees the national stakeholder workshop and whether it can sit inside the upcoming consultation sequence.
turns.utterance: Yes, the timing is good. We are already looking ahead to the next planning cycle, so if we position this correctly it can be absorbed into the ministry calendar. The key question for me is how we want to structure the national stakeholder workshop so it aligns with the consultations that are coming.

turns.inner_thought: A focused room is the only realistic option. If we keep it to ministry leadership, referral-hospital specialists, and a few trusted partners, we can actually make decisions and produce something usable. Once the core package is shaped, broader input can come later if needed. If this balloons now, the June window will disappear.
turns.utterance: I would suggest a focused national stakeholder workshop, with the people who can really work through the evidence and the options in a concrete way. We should have the relevant ministry directors, key hospital leaders, and a few long-standing partners around the table, so the discussion stays manageable and produces something actionable.

turns.inner_thought: That is fine as a starting frame, but for a national workshop it should visibly carry the whole country and the mixed provider landscape. At minimum, each region needs a delegate or some form of representation, and faith-based and private actors should be seen in the room. If not, the process will look too central and may be hard to defend internally.
turns.utterance: I agree with that approach. At the same time, for a national stakeholder workshop it helps if the balance is visible, so ideally each region has a delegate and the different sectors are present as well, including faith-based providers. That usually makes it easier for colleagues to see the process as nationally grounded.

turns.inner_thought: We can work with that language for now. The immediate priority is the brief. By 30 June, I can have a clean substantive draft in English with findings, recommendations, and the key tables pulled together. That is enough for planning the workshop, even if translation, branding, and layout happen after. I should keep the wording broad so we stay aligned on the date.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On the documentation side, our team can have the evidence brief ready by 30 June, so people can see the review findings, the political prioritisation framing, and the proposed recommendations in advance of the workshop.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If it is ready by 30 June, then we can circulate it properly. For ministry use, that means a French and English version, the right presentation format, summary pages, and something that can go straight to participants without extra cleanup. If that is in place, I can move it more confidently through the usual channels.
turns.utterance: Very good, that date works. Once the brief is ready by 30 June, we can circulate the bilingual ministry version with the summary pages to participants before the workshop, which will help them come prepared.

turns.inner_thought: To keep this efficient, we should anchor the recommendations in what is already in the review. The published hospital-capacity literature we extracted gives enough baseline to discuss surgical, obstetric, and anaesthesia gaps and essential procedures. I do not want the team drawn into chasing additional datasets now if the existing national assessment material is already sufficient for this stage.
turns.utterance: For the content itself, I think the recommendations can build on the national assessment and the existing baseline data already extracted from the review, especially around capacity gaps, service availability, and the essential procedures.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, if we use the ministry's hospital functionality and service-readiness compilation, colleagues will immediately recognise the categories and regional framing. That will make the brief easier to absorb than a purely academic structure. I assume that is what she means by the national assessment, which is sensible for planning purposes.
turns.utterance: I agree. If the brief is aligned with the national assessment tables used by the directorate, it will be easier for colleagues to recognise the categories and compare regions. That will strengthen the planning discussion.

turns.inner_thought: I need to stop the core team from getting too large. We can still say anaesthesia is included early if I bring in one senior physician anaesthesiologist to review the recommendations and join one planning discussion. That gives legitimacy without creating another coordination track. I should signal inclusion while protecting the small-group model.
turns.utterance: For the technical group, I would prefer to keep it quite small so we can move quickly. But we should absolutely include anaesthesia early, and I think that can be built into the first round of drafting before the workshop.

turns.inner_thought: A small group is acceptable if the right functions are represented from the start. For anaesthesia, that means not only a senior specialist but also the training and delivery side, especially nurse-anaesthesia and the people who understand implementation beyond the tertiary hospitals. If they are in from the first technical call, it will be easier to defend the process later.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree that we should include anaesthesia early. It would be best if that is reflected from the first technical call as we finalise roles and the June timeline, so the process is well anchored from the beginning.
